question: Luke says Jesus was born during a census taken while Quirinius governed Syria. Josephus dates that census to AD 6, about ten years after Herod died. Didn't Luke get it wrong?

ledger.heading: Fifteenth run (2026-11-20): an independent editor's read of the jesus area, and the area "Contradictions and hard passages"

shortAnswer: On the evidence historians can weigh, he may have, and an honest answer has to say so. Luke places Jesus' birth "in the time of Herod king of Judea" and ties it to "the first census to take place while Quirinius was governor of Syria." Josephus, our fullest source for the period, says Quirinius came to take the census of Judea after Herod's son Archelaus was deposed, a date that works out to AD 6, while Herod died, on the usual reckoning, in 4 BC. No ancient source outside Luke, and the Christian writers who follow him, describes an earlier census in Herod's kingdom. Several solutions have been proposed: a different reading of Luke's Greek, an earlier office for Quirinius, a registration begun under Herod and finished later, a later date for Herod's death. Each has defenders, each has a real weakness, and none commands general agreement. The question is open. What it touches is the date of a census, not whether Jesus was born under Herod in David's town.

sections.heading: The objection at its strongest
sections.body:
The objection rests on the best source we have outside the New Testament, and it was set out most fully in the nineteenth century by Emil Schürer, whose objections a Catholic reference work of 1910 called "a formidable array." Its most careful modern statement is Raymond Brown's *The Birth of the Messiah* (1977), and Joseph Fitzmyer reached the same conclusion in his commentary on Luke (1981).

Josephus tells the story plainly. In the tenth year of Archelaus's government, Augustus deposed him, and "Archelaus's country was laid to the province of Syria; and Cyrenius, one that had been consul, was sent by Cæsar to take account of people's effects in Syria" (*Antiquities* 17.355, in William Whiston's translation, where Cyrenius is Quirinius). Quirinius "came himself into Judea, which was now added to the province of Syria, to take an account of their substance" (18.2). The census provoked the revolt of Judas the Galilean, whom Acts also remembers as rising "in the days of the census" (Acts 5:37, BSB), and Josephus dates the end of the taxing to "the thirty-seventh year of Cæsar's victory over Antony at Actium" (18.26). Actium was fought in 31 BC, so the census belongs to AD 6 or 7.

Luke, by contrast, sets the birth in Herod's lifetime. His story opens "In the time of Herod king of Judea" (Luke 1:5, BSB), and the birth follows within the year. Matthew agrees: "After Jesus was born in Bethlehem in Judea, during the time of King Herod" (Matthew 2:1, BSB). Herod, on the usual reckoning from Josephus, died in 4 BC. So, the critics argue, Luke has a decade's gap he can't close. They add three further points. While Herod lived, Judea was a client kingdom, not a Roman province, and Rome did not usually take censuses in a client king's realm. No source outside Luke mentions a Roman census there before AD 6. And a registration in which "everyone went to his own town to register" (Luke 2:3, BSB) is not attested as Roman practice. The simplest explanation, on this view, is that Luke knew of the famous census and placed the birth by it, a decade too early.

sections.heading: What is true in it
sections.body:
Most of it. The dates are as the critics give them: Josephus is clear that Quirinius's census of Judea followed the deposition of Archelaus, and Luke is clear that Jesus was born under Herod the Great. Luke's own chronology points the same way, since he says Jesus was "about thirty years old" (Luke 3:23, BSB) when he began his work after the fifteenth year of Tiberius, around AD 28 or 29, which puts the birth in Herod's last years, not in AD 6. The difficulty can't be blamed on a copyist; the Study Bible's note on Luke 2 records that no manuscript alters Quirinius's name or the word "first." No surviving source describes a Roman census in Herod's kingdom.

Christians have sometimes claimed far more than the evidence allows. The same Catholic reference work of 1910 said that William Ramsay had shown that Schürer's objections "all fall to the ground." They haven't. Ramsay's arguments are still worth reading, and some of them still have defenders, but the evidence now available doesn't allow anyone to say the question is closed in Luke's favor, and a reader who was told it was has been misled.

sections.heading: The evidence
sections.body:
Begin with what is not in dispute. Augustus did count his subjects. His own record of his reign lists three censuses of Roman citizens, in 28 BC, 8 BC and AD 14, and provincial counts for tribute were taken in Gaul, Egypt and elsewhere. In Roman Egypt households registered every fourteen years, and an edict of the prefect Gaius Vibius Maximus in AD 104 told people living away from home to return to their own districts for the count. A tombstone now in Venice records a census that Quirinius himself ordered at Apamea in Syria. Herod, though a king, was Rome's client, and near the end of his reign Josephus reports that "all the people of the Jews gave assurance of their good-will to Cæsar, and to the king's government," while more than six thousand Pharisees refused to swear (*Antiquities* 17.42). None of this is the census Luke describes, but it shows the kind of world in which one could happen.

Then the governors. Josephus names Saturninus and Volumnius as "the presidents of Syria" in the years before Herod's death (*Antiquities*, book 16), and Quintilius Varus as president of Syria when Herod died. Quirinius doesn't appear in that office until AD 6. Christian writers of the second century did not see the problem as moderns do. Justin Martyr, writing around 155 to the emperor, said the birth could be confirmed "from the registers of the taxing made under Cyrenius, your first procurator in Judæa" (*First Apology* 34, in the Ante-Nicene Fathers translation). Tertullian, early in the third century, wrote that "there is historical proof that at this very time a census had been taken in Judæa by Sentius Saturninus" (*Against Marcion* 4.19, in Holmes's translation in the Ante-Nicene Fathers), naming a governor of Herod's last years rather than Quirinius.

Now the proposed solutions, each with its weakness.

The first is grammatical. Luke's Greek says this registration "took place first" while Quirinius governed Syria. Nigel Turner argued that "first" followed by a genitive can mean "before," giving "this census took place before Quirinius was governor of Syria," to set it apart from the famous one. The grammar is possible, and some careful scholars have adopted it. But most grammarians find it strained, since Luke's construction most naturally says the census happened while Quirinius was governing, and Luke had a plainer word for "before" if he wanted it.

The second proposes an earlier office for Quirinius. Ramsay pointed to an inscription found at Tivoli, near Rome, which records a man who governed Syria a second time; Theodor Mommsen assigned it to Quirinius. If he held some command in Syria before Herod died, Luke's verb, which can describe governing in a general sense, might cover it. The weakness is that the man's name is lost, Ronald Syme and others have assigned the inscription to someone else, and no source says that Quirinius held any office in Syria before AD 6.

The third follows Tertullian. Perhaps a registration was begun under Saturninus or Varus, connected with the oath of loyalty Josephus mentions, and Luke names it by the man under whom the counting became famous. This fits Tertullian's independent-looking tradition and Herod's dependence on Rome. Its weakness is that it is a reconstruction: no source links the oath to a census, and Tertullian may simply have inferred Saturninus from the list of governors.

The fourth moves Herod's death. A minority of scholars, following W. E. Filmer in 1966 and Andrew Steinmann in 2009, date it to 1 BC rather than 4 BC. That helps other parts of the chronology, but it still leaves six or seven years between Herod and Quirinius's census, so it doesn't solve this problem by itself.

The fifth is the critics' own: Luke erred. Its strength is simplicity. Its weakness is that Luke elsewhere handles Roman officials and titles with care, as the Study Bible's notes on Luke 3 and Acts record, and that he plainly knew the census of Judas's revolt as a landmark. Critics reply, fairly, that care elsewhere doesn't guarantee accuracy here.

sections.heading: The argument, laid out
sections.intro: This is an argument about what an unresolved difficulty does and doesn't show.
steps: Luke dates Jesus' birth under Herod the Great and links it to a registration while Quirinius governed Syria; Josephus dates Quirinius's census of Judea to AD 6, after Herod's death; and no ancient source independent of Luke describes an earlier census in Herod's kingdom.

Each proposed reconciliation is possible, but none is established by evidence that historians generally accept, so on present evidence the question is unresolved, and on the historical evidence alone the possibility that Luke misdated the census can't be ruled out.

Whether Jesus was born, of David's line, in the last years of Herod does not hang on the census: Matthew, who on most scholars' view wrote independently of Luke, places the birth under Herod in Bethlehem, and Luke's own chronology of Jesus' ministry points to the same years.
sections.conclusion: So: the census of Quirinius is a real and open difficulty for Luke's dating, which a fair reader should neither explain away nor treat as settled against him, and it leaves the time and setting of Jesus' birth where both Gospels put it.
sections.after: The weight sits on the second step. A reader who finds one of the reconciliations convincing will think the difficulty smaller; a reader who thinks the error view plainly right will think it larger. The step says only that the evidence now available doesn't decide between them, and that is where it should be tested.

sections.heading: The strongest reply, and an answer
sections.body:
The strongest reply is that this is special pleading. If a Roman historian had misdated a famous census by a decade, no one would hesitate to call it an error and lower their trust in him accordingly. Luke tells us he "carefully investigated everything from the beginning" (Luke 1:3, BSB). If he got this wrong, the critic argues, why trust him about a virgin's child, a choir of angels or an empty tomb?

Part of that should be granted. If Luke erred here, he erred, and a Christian shouldn't use a softer standard for Luke than for Tacitus. But the standard historians actually use is not that one mistake discredits a writer. Ancient historians differ with one another on dates and details, and historians weigh each claim on its own evidence; this library's page on the four Easter accounts sets out how Tacitus and Suetonius disagree about the fire of Rome in 64. On that standard Luke's dating of the census is uncertain, while his naming of Herod as king, of Tiberius's fifteenth year, of Pilate, Antipas, Philip and Annas and Caiaphas can be checked against other sources and holds. The claims a skeptic most doubts, the virgin conception and the resurrection, don't rise or fall with a census either. They have to be weighed on their own evidence, which the other pages of this library set out. What the reply does show is that the doctrine of Scripture a Christian holds has to be able to face a passage like this one honestly, and that is where Christians differ.

sections.heading: What remains unresolved
sections.body: The date of the census Luke describes, and whether it can be fitted to Herod's lifetime, is unresolved. So is the exact year of Herod's death, 4 BC on the usual reckoning, 1 BC on a minority view. Whose career the Tivoli inscription records is unknown. Whether Luke's "whole empire" describes a single decree or Augustus's policy of counting his provinces is argued. And whether new evidence will ever settle the matter is unknown. Papyri and inscriptions keep turning up, but none so far has done so.

sections.heading: Where Christians differ
sections.body: Christians answer this passage according to how they confess Scripture's truthfulness, and the site takes no side among them. Christians who hold to inerrancy, in the form the Chicago Statement of 1978 gave it, confess that Scripture in its original writings is without error in all that it affirms, history included. They hold that Luke's statement is true when rightly understood, favor one of the reconciliations above or hold the question in suspense, and follow the Statement's fourteenth article: "We deny that alleged errors and discrepancies that have not yet been resolved vitiate the truth claims of the Bible." Christians who hold Scripture to be infallible in what God gave it to teach, the way of salvation and of life with him, hold that a misdated census would not touch that teaching, and some of them think Luke did misdate it. Both confess together, with the Nicene Creed, that the Holy Spirit "spake by the prophets," and both receive Scripture as the church's final authority for faith and life. All of them confess with the creeds that the Son of God was born of the Virgin Mary, a real child in real history.

claims.claim: Luke dated Jesus' birth by the census of Quirinius, which Josephus places in AD 6, a decade after Herod died, so Luke misdated it
The census of Luke 2 is the famous census of AD 6, placed a decade too early
